card.greeting: Welcome aboard, dear traveler; let us prepare you for a gracious business dinner in Seoul.
card.title: Business dinner with a client’s boss in Seoul
card.closing: Thank you for traveling with me, dear traveler; your host’s own guidance should always take precedence.

raw_tips.tip: It is considered courteous to greet your host with a bow; if you shake hands, support your right forearm with your left hand.
raw_tips.evidence: The bow is the traditional Korean greeting, although it is often accompanied by a handshake among men. To show respect when shaking hands, support your right forearm with your left hand.

raw_tips.tip: It is considered more courteous to keep your rice bowl on the table rather than lifting it to your mouth.
raw_tips.evidence: Unlike the Chinese or Japanese, South Koreans never raise a rice bowl to their mouth. During a meal, bowls and dishes remain on the table.

raw_tips.tip: Please avoid standing chopsticks upright in rice or other food.
raw_tips.evidence: Chopsticks may be put down on a table or on a purpose designed chopstick rest, but never put into food standing up, particularly rice

raw_tips.tip: If alcohol is offered, receive the cup with both hands and a slight bow, particularly when accepting from an elder or senior host.
raw_tips.evidence: When receiving a cup from an elder, one must hold it with two hands (left palm at the bottom and holding the cup with the right hand) and bow their head slightly.

raw_tips.tip: Offer to pour for your host and attend to others’ glasses rather than pouring only for yourself.
raw_tips.evidence: It is generally preferred that hosts fill the drinks of their company, and the company should do the same for the host.

raw_tips.tip: If you need to blow your nose, it is considered more courteous to step away from the table or be discreet.
raw_tips.evidence: If such an action is necessary, it is recommended to leave the table or otherwise be discreet.
